rewrite.question: A function returns `{ id: 1, tags: ['new'] }`. The test compares it with an object literal written inside the test. Which Jest matcher passes?
rewrite.hint: The expected object is constructed in the test, so it is not the same object the function returned. Which comparison survives that?
rewrite.explanation: `toEqual` walks both values and compares them property by property, so two separately built objects with the same contents pass. `toBe` calls `Object.is`, which compares identity: the literal written in the test is a different object, so it fails even though every field matches. `toContain` checks membership in an array or string, and `toThrow` checks that a call raises.

rationale: Worth redistributing to nodejs, level 24 'Testing & Debugging': the identity-versus-structure trap is the one assertion mistake beginners hit on their first object test, and it is the same lesson as assert.strictEqual versus assert.deepStrictEqual in node:test. rewrite.question: `parse('bad')` throws. Which assertion reports that the call throws, instead of failing with the error itself?
options: expect(parse('bad')).toThrow()
expect(() => parse('bad')).toThrow()
expect(parse('bad')).toEqual(new Error('bad'))
expect(parse('bad')).toBeInstanceOf(Error)
rewrite.hint: Whatever you hand to `expect` is evaluated first. Ask where the error goes before any matcher runs.
rewrite.explanation: `toThrow` needs a function it can call inside its own try/catch, so the failing call has to be wrapped: `expect(() => parse('bad')).toThrow()`. Writing `expect(parse('bad'))` evaluates the call first, the error escapes past `expect`, and the test fails with that raw error rather than reporting a satisfied expectation. Jest's documentation states it directly: 'You must wrap the code in a function, otherwise the error will not be caught and the assertion will fail.' Matchers that compare a returned value cannot help, because a throwing call returns nothing.

rationale: Worth redistributing to nodejs, level 24 'Testing & Debugging': the wrapper requirement is a real first-week mistake in Jest, Vitest and node:test alike, and the current options waste it on throwaway matchers. Rewritten, every distractor encodes the same live misconception at a different angle.
evidence: node: assert.throws(boom, RangeError) passes, while assert.throws(boom(), RangeError) lets the RangeError escape before the assertion runs (node --test, 13/13 pass)
https://jestjs.io/docs/expect — '.toThrow()': 'You must wrap the code in a function, otherwise the error will not be caught and the assertion will fail.'

rewrite.question: A spy is created once for a whole test file. The second test asserts it was called exactly once and passes only when it runs alone. What does clearing the spy between tests fix?
options: Call history left by the earlier test, which makes the later assertion depend on run order
The original implementation the spy replaced, which otherwise stays swapped out
The time the spy adds to the run, because a cleared spy records nothing
The coverage total, which otherwise counts each spied call twice
rewrite.hint: Two tests, one spy. Ask what the spy still remembers when the second test starts.
rewrite.explanation: A spy keeps its recorded calls until something clears them, so the second test sees the first test's call, counts two, and passes only when it runs on its own. Clearing between tests (Jest's `jest.clearAllMocks`, Vitest's `vi.clearAllMocks`, `mock.resetCalls()` in node:test) drops that history while leaving the replacement in place. Putting the original implementation back is a separate step — `restoreAllMocks` — so the second option describes a different operation, not what clearing does.

rationale: Worth redistributing to nodejs, level 24 'Testing & Debugging': leaked call history is a concrete order-dependence cause that rm-general-138 only diagnoses in the abstract, and the clear-versus-restore distinction is runner API knowledge that belongs with the runner. The rewrite turns the instruction into the symptom and gives every distractor a real misconception.
evidence: node: a mock.fn keeps callCount() at 2 across calls until mock.resetCalls() drops it back to 0 (node --test, 13/13 pass)

https://jestjs.io/docs/jest-object — jest.clearAllMocks() 'Clears the mock.calls, mock.instances, mock.contexts and mock.results properties of all mocks'; restoreAllMocks 'Restores all mocks and replaced properties back to their original value'

rewrite.question: An integration suite inserts and deletes rows on every run. Where should it point its database connection?
options: At production, so the data the tests see is realistic
At a database created for the run, such as a container or a per-suite schema
At the shared staging database the team also uses by hand
At no database at all, with every query replaced by a stub
rewrite.hint: The suite writes and deletes rows. Ask who else is reading that data while the tests run.
rewrite.explanation: A database created for the run belongs to that run alone, so the suite can insert, delete and reset freely and two runs cannot collide. Production is never an option for a suite that writes. Shared staging is the tempting middle answer and the one that causes trouble: another engineer's manual edit changes what the tests see, which is a common source of failures that nobody can reproduce. Stubbing every query removes the database entirely, which leaves an integration test with nothing to integrate.

rewrite.question: An integration suite opens a transaction before each test and rolls it back afterward. What does that arrangement actually buy?
options: Each test's writes disappear at rollback, so the next test starts from the same data
Rolled-back writes never reach disk, so the suite needs less storage
The commit path the code runs in production is exercised end to end
In-process fixtures shared between tests are reset along with the rows
rewrite.hint: Ask what the next test finds in the tables once the transaction has been rolled back.
rewrite.explanation: Rolling back discards the rows a test wrote, so every test starts from the same fixture without truncating tables or re-seeding — cheap isolation for a database suite. It does not exercise commit: in PostgreSQL a BEGIN issued inside an open transaction only warns and leaves the transaction state unaffected, so code that commits on its own ends the wrapping transaction and its writes survive. A database rollback also leaves in-process state such as caches and module-level fixtures untouched.

rationale: Worth redistributing to databases, level 11 'Transactions & ACID': the rollback-per-test pattern is a real use of transaction semantics and is distinct from rm-general-143, whose fix is giving each test its own data. The rewrite supplies the missing caveats — self-committing code and in-process state — as the distractors.
evidence: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-begin.html — 'Issuing BEGIN when already inside a transaction block will provoke a warning message. The state of the transaction is not affected.'; nesting requires savepoints
knowledge: rolling back a per-test transaction removes that test's rows without truncating or re-seeding the tables
